data.copy:
My husband called me lazy for six years. My doctor said it was probably depression. My mother told me to just "push through it." Turns out the reason I could barely function had nothing to do with my mindset, it was living in my mattress.

I need to tell you this because I wish someone had told me years ago.

Every single morning for the last six years, I woke up feeling like I'd been hit by a truck. Blocked nose. Dry throat. 

Eyes so puffy my daughter once asked if I'd been crying in my sleep.

And the tiredness. God, the tiredness.
Not regular tired. The kind of tired where you make breakfast and then have to sit down for twenty minutes before you can clean up. 

The kind where you cancel lunch with your best friend, again, because the thought of showering, getting dressed, and driving across town makes you want to cry.

I stopped going to book club. Stopped walking the dog. Stopped volunteering at the school canteen because I couldn't trust myself to stay upright for a full shift.
I was 65 and I genuinely believed my life was winding down.

Ray thought I was being dramatic. "You're always tired," he'd say, like it was a character flaw. My GP ran bloods, thyroid, iron, B12, glucose, the lot. Everything came back normal. She put me on antidepressants. 

I took them for eight months. They just made me foggy and tired.

So I did what I think a lot of us do. I accepted it. This is what 65 feels like. Some people get more energy and others get less and I got less and that's just how it is.
I want you to know that thought "this is just my life now" is the most dangerous lie I ever told myself.

Because the whole time, something else was going on.
It started with a cough. Not a cold cough, a dry, scratchy, 5:30am cough that hit me within minutes of waking up. 

Every. Single. Morning. 

Ray didn't have it. Just me. I'd cough, blow my nose, hack up something awful, and then spend the next two hours feeling like I was breathing through a wet towel.

data.copy:
It was 11:47 PM when I found my mom collapsed on the bathroom floor, gasping for air like she was drowning on dry land.

I'm Tyler, a 22-year-old engineering student from Florida. All my life, I'd been watching my mom slowly kill herself with cigarettes, but that night in March changed everything.

Mom had been a pack-a-day smoker for 18 years. Started in college, just like I was now. "Just socially," she used to say. "I can quit anytime."

We'd tried everything. Nicotine patches that gave her rashes. Gum that made her nauseous. Vapes that she claimed "just weren't the same." Cold turkey attempts that lasted maybe 36 hours before the shaking and irritability became unbearable.

But that Tuesday night was different.

I'd come home late from the engineering lab to find her wheezing on the couch, her face slightly blue-tinged in the TV light.

"Mom, you okay?" I asked, already knowing the answer.

She waved me off, trying to speak but only managing a rattling cough that sounded like gravel in a blender.

By 11 PM, the coughing hadn't stopped. By 11:30, she was struggling to walk to the bathroom. By 11:47, I was calling 911 while she clutched her chest on the cold tile floor.

The ER doctor's words still echo in my mind: "Stage 2 lung cancer. We caught it early enough to treat, but she needs to quit smoking immediately. Not reduce. Not switch to vaping. Quit completely."

Mom survived. The treatments were brutal – chemotherapy that left her exhausted, radiation that burned her throat, surgery that removed part of her left lung.

data.copy:
I tried every internet hack for water rings for 3 years straight.

Toothpaste.

Mayo.

The iron trick.

Vinegar and oil.

Then a furniture restorer told me why NONE of them actually work.

I'm 41 years old.

I've owned my dining table for 9 years.

It's solid oak.

Cost me $2,400.

And for the last three years, it's had a white ring right in the center where my husband set down a hot casserole dish without a trivet.

The moment I saw that ring, I went straight to Google.

"How to remove heat marks from wood table."

The internet had answers.

Lots of them.

I tried the iron trick first.

Put a towel over the ring.

Set the iron on low.

Moved it in circles.

At first, it seemed to work.

The ring faded a little.

But the next morning?

It was back.

Maybe even worse.

I tried the mayonnaise method next.

Slathered it on.

Left it overnight like the blog said.

Wiped it off in the morning.

Nothing.

Just a greasy table that smelled like a sandwich.

Then I tried the toothpaste method.

Non-gel, like everyone specified.

Rubbed it in with a soft cloth for twenty minutes.

My arm was sore.

The ring was still there.

I tried oil and vinegar.

I tried walnut meat rubbed over the surface.

I tried a store-bought "water ring remover" cloth that cost me $8 and required "10+ minutes of serious elbow grease."

I rubbed for fifteen minutes.

My table looked shinier.

But the ring?

Still there.

Mocking me.

After three years of trying every hack the internet offered, I'd accepted defeat.

That ring was part of my table now.

I stopped inviting people over for dinner.

Not because of the ring itself.

But because every time someone noticed it, I had to explain.

And every explanation felt like admitting I couldn't fix something in my own home.

Then, last fall, I took a chair to a local furniture restorer for reupholstering.

While I was there, I mentioned my table.

Told him about the ring.

About everything I'd tried.

He laughed.

Not meanly.

More like recognition.

data.copy:
I knew my periods would stop. I expected that.

I knew there might be hot flashes. I bought a fan.

I knew I might gain a few pounds. I bought bigger jeans.

I knew there might be some moodiness — that's what every article I'd read called it. Moodiness. Like teenage moodiness. Like "I'm a little snippy this week."

Nobody warned me about the rage.

Nobody warned me my sleep would be this bad. That I'd wake at 3am and lie there until the alarm went off, every single night, for years.

Nobody warned me I'd scream at my eighteen-year-old daughter over a question about a mattress protector.

Nobody warned me my husband would start reading me carefully before he spoke — the way you read a stranger you don't quite trust yet.

Nobody warned me my own daughter would start calling her father, not me, when she had a hard day at school. Because she didn't know which version of me she'd get.

Nobody warned me I'd wake at 3am replaying every cruel thing I'd said the day before, promise myself I'd do better, and snap by 4pm at something just as small.

Nobody told me my temper would do this. Nobody told me I would, slowly and quietly, become a mother my children were scared of.

I'm 55. I've been doing this for eight years.

My name is Elaine Walker. I have what doctors call "mood symptoms of menopause." What I call eight years of becoming a person I do not recognize.

Most days look the same.

3:14am, my eyes open. I lie there until the alarm goes off at 6.

data.copy:
My Blood Pressure Was 158/94. My GP Prescribed Ramipril. Five Months Later, It's 124/78. I Never Filled the Prescription.

I've been a nurse for 32 years.

I've watched hundreds of patients start blood pressure medication. ACE inhibitors, usually. Ramipril, Lisinopril, Perindopril. The "gold standard," GPs call it.

I've also watched what happens to them over the years that follow.

The dizziness that never goes away. That light-headed, unsteady feeling that makes them hold onto walls when they stand up. "I feel like I'm going to faint," they tell me. "Just getting out of bed scares me."

The exhaustion that steals their energy. Patients who used to be active and capable—now struggling to get through the day, napping by 2pm, cancelling plans because they're too drained.

The persistent dry cough. That irritating hack that wakes them at night, embarrasses them in public, never fully resolves no matter what they try.

The brain fog that clouds their thinking. Patients who were sharp and engaged—now forgetting appointments, losing words mid-sentence, struggling to concentrate.

And the creeping dependence. One medication becomes two. Then three. The doses increase. The side effects compound. And their blood pressure never truly stabilises—it just gets chemically suppressed whilst their vessels continue to stiffen underneath.

The medical literature calls these "well-tolerated side effects." But in my experience, patients aren't tolerating them. They're suffering. They just don't realise there might be another way.

So when my own blood pressure started creeping up—148/88, then 152/90, then 158/94—and my GP mentioned starting Ramipril, I smiled politely and said I'd think about it.

But I already knew I wasn't going to take it.

I'd seen too much. I wasn't going down that road.

minadspend.description: Minimum EU ad spend total in adspendtimeframe window.
minadspend.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. May require higher account tier; can return upgrade JSON.

maxadspend.description: Maximum EU ad spend in window.
maxadspend.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. 999999 treated as no upper cap server-side.

adspendtimeframe.description: Rolling window ad spend is summed over (NOT a calendar month filter).

minreach.description: Minimum EU reach/views total in reachtimeframe window.
minreach.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. May require higher account tier.

reachtimeframe.description: Rolling window reach is summed over.

mintraffic.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. May require higher account tier.

minproductsonstore.description: Minimum published products on the Shopify store.

minprice.description: Minimum product price on landing page.

mincopylength.description: Minimum ad primary text character length.

minvideolength.description: Minimum video duration in seconds (use with mediafilter=videos).

mindays.description: Minimum days the ad has been running.
mindays.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. May require higher account tier.

from.description: Ad launch date lower bound (Meta started field — when ad began running, NOT scrape date).
from.allowed_values: YYYY-MM-DD. Requires to on same range.

to.notes: To isolate ads running in a calendar month: ad_created_to=last day of month AND fromlastseen=first day of month.

product_from.description: Shopify product creation date lower bound.

pagefrom.description: Facebook page creation date lower bound.

activestatus.description: Legacy dashboard param (no longer applied to ES queries).
activestatus.allowed_values: Ignored — use adstatus or last_seen_from/to instead.

adstatus.description: Dashboard Status filter — recently seen vs stale ads.
adstatus.allowed_values: active (lastSeen or updated_at within last 4 days), inactive (neither field within last 4 days), All/empty (no status filter).
adstatus.notes: find_winning_products forces active. Same as dashboard Status = Active.

sorting.allowed_values: relevance, datefound, mostrecent, lastseen, adspend, longestrunning, reach, adsetamount, consistency, monthlyvisits, monthlytraffic, monthlyrevenue, pageactiveads, toprank, mostsaved. Aliases: rank/top_ad/best_ranked→toprank (asc = best rank first, desc = worst rank first). ad_started→mostrecent. monthly_visits→monthlyvisits. monthly_traffic→monthlytraffic.

page.description: Pagination page index (informational). Deep pagination requires scroll from the previous response — incrementing page alone does not advance the result set.
page.allowed_values: MCP uses 1-based page (1=first page); echoed value is 0-based internal page sent to API.

scroll.description: Opaque pagination cursor. Empty/omit on the first request; pass the response scroll value on the next request with the same filters to fetch more ads. Required to download beyond the first page (especially sort_by=lastseen).
scroll.allowed_values: Opaque string from previous response; empty string or omit for first page. Stop when scroll is null/absent or data is shorter than a full page.

mcp_pagination.hint: Pass scroll_next as scroll on the next call with the same filters to continue. Do not rely on page alone.
